A Modular Synthesis of Antitumor Macrolide (–)-Lasonolide A† 
Lin Yang,a,b Zuming Lin,a Kuan Zheng,a,b Luyao Kong,a,b and Ran Hong*,a 
a CAS Key Laboratory of Synthetic Chemistry of Natural Substances, Center for Excellence in Molecular Synthesis, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, 
Chinese Academy of Sciences, 345 Lingling Road, Shanghai 200032, China 
b University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, 19A Yuquan Road, Beijing 100049, China 
Cite this paper: Chin. J. Chem. 2020, 38, 725—736. DOI: 10.1002/cjoc.202000026 
Summary of main observation and conclusion  Lasonolide A was identified as a potent antitumor macrolide towards various cancer cell lines. The two 
tetrahydropyrans bearing multiple stereogenic centers as well as the polyene linkage attracted a dozen synthetic research groups to launch the total syn-
thesis. Based on the synthetic methods developed in our group, namely, the hydroboration of allene and its subsequent allylation as well as the iterative 
hydroboration of allene and oxidation, the polyol subunits were efficiently constructed and then integrated into the final ta rget. A new Julia olefination 
reagent, double-headed sulfone, was designed to promote the rapid coupling  of two aldehydes bearing multiple functional groups to secure the whole 
carbon framework. Another highlight of our approach is the application of a traceless protecting group, 9-BBN (9-borabicyclo[3.3.1]nonane), to hide the 
secondary alcohol for debenzylation, and for the first time, to mask the carboxylic acid for Julia olefination under strong basic conditions. 
 
Background and Originality Content 
Marine natural products have emerged as a rich resource for 
drug discovery due to their fascinating structures and various 
biological activities. Since the first FDA -approved marine natural 
product-derived Ziconotide, an atypical analgesic agent for the 
amelioration of severe and chronic pain, dozens of marine natural 
products have been developed for clinical use. [1] Among the 
structurally diverse compounds isolated from the deep sea , 
polyketide plays a pivotal role in the development of marine 
drugs. A milestone in drug discovery is t he development of 
Halaven® (eribulin mesylate) , which is clinically used for the 
treatment of metastatic breast cancer. [2] Although this marketed 
drug is a truncation of the marine natural product h alichondrin B, 
the formidable complexity of its chemical s tructure remains a 
synthetic challenge because the sample supply relies only on its 
total synthesis in the laboratory. [2b] To quickly provide sufficient 
materials of promising leads such as halichondrin B and embark 
on the medicinal studies of their deriva tives, novel synthetic 
methods and strategies are still in high demand. 
In the continuing interest in the field of polyketide synthesis, 
our laboratory has embarked on the development of novel 
methods and efficient strategies to assemble complex bioactive 
polyketides.[3] During the hydroboration of allenic alcohol 1 
(Scheme 1), we noticed a selection of different alkylboranes 
would provide various 1,3 -diols 2 in a highly diastereoselective 
manner after the allylation of the aldehydes, which were at -
tributed to the stereodefined E- or Z-allyboranes derived from the 
hydroboration of allenes. Moreover, a generally found boratropic 
rearrangement ([1,3] -boratropic shift) [4] in allylboranes was 
largely suppressed due to the steric bulkiness of the alkyl su bstit-
uents on boron. The superior reactivity of disiamylborane (Sia2BH) 
to the alkene (the terminal olefin in allenes) and the slow 1,3-shift 
of boron facilitate the kinetic hydroboration -allylation to deliver 
an anti,anti-1,3-diol motif with an all-carbon quaternary center.[3c] 
Moreover, the subsequent transformations, including a bidirec -
tional oxa -Michael cyclization, were able to produce diastereo -
isomers of tetrahydropyrans 3 in just 3—4 steps with excellent 
overall yields. 
Scheme 1  Our previous approach to construct tetrahedropyrans (3) 
 
The construction of a variety of tetrahydropyrans (THPs) 
bearing multiple stereocenters encouraged us to devise an effi -
cient modular synthesis for lasonolide A ( 4), a marine polyketide 
featuring two characteristic THP rings. In 1994, McConnell and 
co-workers reported lasonolide A, a complex macrolide exhibiting 
a potent antitumor activity isolated from the Caribbean orange - 
red marine sponge, Forcepia sp. (Figure 1). [5] The originally pro-
posed structure was later revised to be 5 on the basis of the  
 
Figure 1  Structural revision of lasonolide A (4 vs 5).

collective syntheses of diastereoisomers by the Lee group. [6] Oth-
er lasonolide congeners were determined from the same marine 
species by Wright and co -workers in 2004. [7] A comparison of the 
antitumor activities of these marine polyketides revealed the 
crucial role of the ester chain. The potent biological activity [8] and 
intriguing chemical structure attracted many synthetic groups to 
embark on the total synthesis of lasonolides. [9,10] It is particularly 
noteworthy that the Trost group described a 16 -LLS (longest line-
ar sequence, LLS) synthesis of lasonolide A featuring a remarkable  
Ru-catalyzed alkene-alkyne coupling in a highly convergent man -
ner.[9f,g] However, an unsatisfactory regioselectivity in the enyne 
coupling (the ratio of linear/branch: 2/1 —3/1) might be a chal -
lenge for scaling up the synthesis. With these observations i n 
mind, we commenced to devise a novel strategy to produce l a-
sonolide A that is amenable for derivatization for future medicinal 
studies. 
Our retrosynthetic analysis is depicted in Scheme 2. The dis -
connection of the olefin at different sites leads to five  readily 
accessible building blocks 6—10, which could be generally pre -
pared within 4 —8 steps from commercially available materials. 
The unprecedented bissulfone 8 could be derived from subse -
quent Mitsunobu reactions of propan -1,3-diol with PTSH 
(5-mercapto-1-phenyl-1H-tetrazole) and BTSH ( 2-mercaptobenzo-
thiazole). All of the olefination processes would produce the req -
uisite alkenes in a stereodefined manner. The key element to this 
synthetic design is the construction of two tetrahydropyrans 
bearing four stereogenic centers. The method we relied on is an 
oxa-Michael cyclization under thermodynamic control to secure 
the cis-configuration of C7/C11 and C19/C23. Herein, we describe 
the full details of the synthesis of macrolide lasonolide A.[11] 
Scheme 2  Retrosynthetic analysis of (–)-lasonolide A (5) 
 
Results and Discussion 
Syntheses of the two tetrahydropyran rings 
Enantio-integration. The hidden symmetry within the two tet-
rahydropyrans A and B ( 7 and 10) permits us to  devise a novel 
strategy to access such multifunctional subunits (Figure 2). We 
envisioned that both enantiomers of racemic allenic alcohol can 
be evolved to form the individual fragments (Scheme 3). Follow -
ing our previous exploration on the construction of tetrahydro -
pyrans,[3c] the quaternary carbon center in the A -ring could be 
derived from the hydroboration-allylation of R-11, while the ace -
tate form of S-antipode 12 is engaged into the preparation of the 
B-ring ( vide infra ). However, the latter clearly requires an un -
precedented sequential oxidation to install two hydroxy groups in 
a stereoselective manner. According to conventional enantiocon -
vergent synthesis,[12] the S-antipode is likely to be converted into 
the same key intermediate derived f rom the R-enantiomer. Thus, 
in our case, the novel enantio-integrative approach can be con -
sidered to be a chirality-economic process.[13] 
 
Figure 2  The hidden symmetry between 7 and 10. 
Scheme 3  The chirality-economic enantio-integrative approach 
 
A-ring synthesis . Based on our previous work, [3c] a similar 
route toward the A -ring could be devised with oxa -Michael cy -
clization as a key transformation; however, the additional carbon 
chain derived from the Michael addition of the α,β -unsaturated 
ester (as 3 shown in Scheme 1) has to be adjusted to furnish the 
double bond between C17—C18 (Scheme 2). Therefore, a nitro -
olefin was proposed as an alternative Michael acceptor , because 
an aldehyde can be exposed from the nitro group via the Nef 
reaction. A challenge to implement this functional group trans -
formation is that, under basic or acidic conditions, the Nef reac -
tion may induce a severe epimerization of the chirality at the 
α-position of the aldehyde. Little was known about the feasibility 
of using such a strategy in the THP -ring formation with high dia -
stereoselectivity.[14] The only tractable case was reported by the  
Petruš group, in which a pair of 1/1 diastereoisomers was formed 
after a cascade process that included the oxa -Michael addition of 
the nitro-olefin and Nef reaction to form the acetal group.[15] 
The synthesis commenced from allenic alcohol 11, a highly 
optically pure (>99% ee) building block derived from an enzymatic 
kinetic resolution by lipase AK. [16] The recovered R-enantiomer of 
allenic alcohol was first subjected to hydroboration with disiamyl -
borane (Sia 2BH). The resulting Z-allylborane further react ed with 
aldehyde 13 via a kinetic control to give anti,anti-1,3-diol 14 as a 
single stereoisomer (Scheme 4). The configuration of the 1,3 -diol 
was established by Rychnovsky’s method [17] and was consistent 
with the requisite stereochemistry in the A -ring. Consequently, 
masking the 1,3-diol in the presence of camphorsulfonic acid (CSA) 
and subsequently removing the tert-butyldiphenylsilyl (BPS) 
group with TBAF produced a quantitative yield  of 15 bearing a 
primary alcohol. After treatment with 2,2,6,6 -tetramethylpiperi-
dinyloxy (TEMPO) and bis(acetoxy)iodobenzene (BAIB), [18] the 
resultant aldehyde was immediately subjected to the Henry reac -
tion to react with nitromethane in the presence of tetramethyl-
guanidine (TMG). The subsequent triethylamine -promoted elimi -
nation of the corresponding mesylate [19] afforded the requisite 
E-nitro olefin 16 in a combined 81% yield. This one -pot protocol 
was operationally simple and a high yield was achieved  on

Synthesis of Antitumor Macrolide (–)-Lasonolide A Chin. J. Chem. 
gram-scale. The standard condition using para-methylphenylsul-
fonic acid (PTSA) to promote the cyclization was remarkable. We 
found a cascade process, including deketalization, oxa -Michael 
cyclization, the Nef reaction, and acetalation of aldehyde in a  
one-pot protocol to result in tetrahydropyran 17 with excellent 
diastereoselectivity (ds >20/1) and isolated yield (82%). The mild 
conditions to realize the Nef reaction was attributed to a thermo -
dynamically favorable formation of the acetal product 17. The 
extensive NOE studies confirmed the cis-configuration of the ste -
reochemistry between C19 and C23. At this stage, the vinyl group 
was readily converted to the hydroxymethyl group through ozo -
nolysis and immediate reduction with NaBH 4. Without further  
purification, the crude mixture was suitable for the subsequent 
selective silylation to form 18 in 90% yield. 
Scheme 4  Preparation of the A-ring acetal 18 
 
The following installation of the ester chain would be con -
venient if the benzyl group is removed. Indeed, debenzylation 
was readily performed under heterogeneous hydrogenation to 
give the primary alcohol 7 with excellent yield (Scheme 5). We 
challenged ourselves to realize such a transformation without 
transition metal catalysis. A transition -metal free synthesis would 
be particularly intriguing in terms of eliminating a tedious purifi -
cation process in the complex molecule synthesis, especially for 
those intermediates or the final product that are in an oil form 
and not purifiable via recrystallization. [20] A lithium -naphthalene 
system[21] was adopted for debenzylation in presence of the silyl 
group. To our surprise, a silyl -migrated product 19 (60% yield)  
Scheme 5  Debenzylation and silyl-migration product 19 
 
caused contamination during the process. A single -crystal analysis 
revealed the structure of 19, in which the silyl group was reloca t-
ed to the secondary alcohol at C21. 
A common solution to suppress t he interference of the prox-
imal C21 -OH is the introduction of another protecting group. 
However, the additional protection -deprotection steps will dra -
matically decrease the synthetic efficacy. [22] The stability of 
borinate (the boron -ate complex) generally encountered in the 
Brown hydroboration-oxidation[23] inspired us to propose borane 
as a traceless protecting group. With the consideration of steric 
hindrance and stability, 9-BBN was defined as the optimal reagent 
of choice. Compound 18 was first treated with 9 -BBN and then 
subjected to debenzylation by lithium naphthalene (Scheme 6). To 
our delight, a clean transformation occurred and the desired 
product 7 was isolated with 91% yield. Consequently, the primary 
alcohol 7 was subjected to  a selective oxidative and immediate 
Wittig reaction with phosphonium salt 6, prepared at the gram - 
scale by Trost’s protocol[9f] to furnish the top fragment 21 at 70% 
isolated yield. The tolerance of the borinate intermediate to lith -
ium-naphthalene would  be valuable in other chemical transfor -
mations. A recent interesting case reported by the Hoveyda group 
also revealed this valuable approach (protection in a borinate 
form) in Mo- or Ru-based ring-closing metathesis (RCM).[24] 
Scheme 6  Preparation of the top fragment 21 
 
B-ring synthesis . Although there is no quaternary carbon 
center in the B -ring, the installation of two hydroxy groups is still 
a difficult task, especially to achieve a good facial selectivity of the 
hydroxylation of the trisubstituted acyclic alkene (Figure 3). 
Brown and co -workers reported an excellent stereoselectivity of 
the hydroboration-oxidation of the cyclic trisubstituted alkene. [25] 
For the acyclic variants, hydroboration is generally slow an d often 
suffers from competing alkene isomerization. Moreover, it is also 
difficult to achieve excellent stereoselectivity due to an A 1,3 
strain.[26] Based on the observations in the various precedents, 
the hydroboration of the E-trisubstituted alkene mainly resulted 
in anti,anti or syn,anti-diastereomers of 1,3 -diols.[27] In a recent 
solution reported by the Evans group, the hydroboration of 
Z-alkene with ThexBH 2 via a bis-alkoxysilane medium 7 -mem-
bered ring resulted in  syn,syn-1,3-triols with excellent diastere o-
selectivity ( ds ≥19 : 1).[28] We thus envisioned that a possible 
boron-ate complex to chelate 1,4 -diol may also promote the 
hydroboration of Z-alkene to favor a syn,syn-isomer through  
 
Figure 3  Synthesis of syn,syn-triol and Evans approach.

mimicking the conformation of the silyl -templated medium ring 
(the chelation model in Figure 3).[29] 
At the outset, a common challenge for the hydroboration of 
trisubstituted alkene was a severe double bond isomerization and 
migration that would scramble the hydroboration/oxidation to 
give a mixture of alcohols.[29] ThexBH2 was selected as the reagent 
due to its superior reactivity for hydroboration of sterically bulky 
alkenes.[30] Formation of bo rinate complex and hydroboration 
with ThexBH2 resulted in the desired triol 23a albeit in an unsatis-
fied diasetereoselectivity ( ds 1.4/1) along with the formation of 
syn-diol 23c[31] (entry 1, Table 1). To improve the selectivity in 
hydroboration, a more sterically demanding Sia2BH may provide a 
confining ate complex, which therefore facilitates the facial selec -
tivity of hydroboration with ThexBH 2. However, this combination 
remained to show a severe isomerization of alkene (entries 2 and 
3, Table 1). Application of a less reactive, and more selective 
9-BBN allowed the subsequent hydroboration occur to deliver the 
triol favoring syn,syn-isomer ( ds 2.5/1) (entry 4). Interestingly, 
decreasing the amount of 9 -BBN further improved the diastereo -
selectivity (ds 4/1) to give syn,syn-triol 23a in 61% isolated yield 
(entry 5). The inherent chirality in the borane reagent would af -
fect the stereoselectivity as well as the conversion (entries 6 —8) 
and identified the optimal conditions of using (+) -IpcBH2 for the 
hydroboration with a synthetically useful yield (76%) (entry 7). 
Although the antipode ( –)-IpcBH2 resulted in a similar diastereo -
selectivity (ds 6.2/1) albeit the slower reaction rate (entry 8) , the 
single borane reagent did not offer a better selectivity (entry 9). 
In our previous work, an acyclic model (Felkin-Ahn-like model) 
was preferentially suggested to decipher the stereochemical out -
come.[11] However, such model remains incomplete to understand 
the deterioration in diastereoselectivity when different sterically 
demanding boranes were applied for the hydroboration. Here, we 
would re-evaluate a chelation model (Figure 4). Interestingly, the 
conventionally adapted Houk model[30e,f] preferred a σ-donor (i.e., 
the R group instead of OH or OR) to be antiperiplanar to the ap -
proaching borane and thus the hydroboration and subsequent 
oxidation will form another diastereoisomer, anti,syn-triol (Figure 
4A). This interpretation is clearly distinct to the current result. We 
noticed that a smooth reaction of borane with alcohol occurred 
when 9-BBN[32] and IpcBH2 were added subsequently. It was thus 
concluded that the borinate complex should be involved in th e 
subsequent hydroboration. This notion was actually pointed out 
in the original Still’s work, in which the formation of borinate 
(alkoxylborane) was found to be more rapidly than the hydrobo -
ration of alkene. [30c] However, a simple modification of the Hou k 
model bearing the two borinate motifs would again deliver the 
anti,syn-isomer (Figure 4B). With the above information in mind, 
a chelation model, derived from the dehydrocoupling of 9 -BBN 
with the primary allylic alcohol and the additional interaction with 
the sterically demanding secondary allylic alcohol, is thus as -
sumed to act (Figure 4C). In this conformation of the borinate 
complex, the sterically bulky R group is pseudo -equatorial, facili-
tating the addition of IpcBH 2 to the least hindered and conv ex 
face of the trisubstituted alkene and thus to afford syn,syn-triol 
23a as the major product. Moreover, an increase of 9 -BBN (>1.5

Following the optimal condition, 2 -Z-Ene-1,4-diol 22 first re -
acted with 9 -BBN (1 equiv) and the proposed boron -ate complex 
was then subjected to another borane reagent for the hydrobora -
tion (IpcBH2, 3.3 equiv in THF). The corresponding triol 23a can be 
obtained in 73% yield and good diastereoselectivity ( ds 6.4/1) 
(Scheme 7). [33] The reaction was readily performed in gram -scale 
and a sufficient material was thus accumulated. 
Scheme 7  Preparation of the B-ring 26 
 
It is noteworthy that the optical purity of the corresponding 
1,4-diol 22 was further enriched up to 99% ee from 95.5% ee after 
recrystallization. It is also important to improve the optical purity 
of the final polyketide target , because most of the intermediates 
are in oil form in total synthesis. The following acid -promoted 
protection of the vicinal diol and subsequent removal of the BPS 
group by TBAF yielded diol 24 in 82% yield. The oxidative Wittig 
reaction secured the Michael acceptor, which allowed the next 
oxa-1,4-addition to form the cis-tetrahydropyran B -ring 26 with 
high diastereoselectivity (ds 11/1) and 82% yield (Table 2). Due to 
the lack of the Thorpe -Ingold effect [34] as that in compound 16 
(Schemes 4), a stronger acid as promoter was required to pro -
mote the requisite cyclization with a good yield and high stereo -
selectivity. PCSA (para-chlorobenzenesulfonic acid) was effective 
to promote the cyclization with a moderate yield (entry 3). Fur -
ther increasing the acidity did not offer a better outcome (entries 
4 and 5). The optimal condition to deliver THP 26 was using 2 
equivalents of PCSA at reflux in EtOH (entry 6). 
Although the standard oxidative Wittig reaction could convert 
diol 26 to a conjugated ester, the severe epimerization at C11 
implicated that the delicate control of the reaction conditions 
would be necessary (entry 1 in Table 3). Therefore, a series of 
TEMPO derivatives, oxidants, and other reaction parameters were 
screened (Table 2). A direct oxidation with DMP did not afford 
any desired product (entry 2). A mild oxidant, TEMPOBF 4, was 
effective to suppress the epimerization (entry 3). By using strong 
oxidant, TCCA, [35] a faster reaction occurred and the ratio was 
improved to 4/1 albeit with a low isolated yield (entry 4). We then 
focused on TEMPO -derivatives. In THF, substitution at C4 ( 27a 
and 27b) delivered a higher ratio albeit a sluggish reaction (en -
tries 5 and 6). The less polar solvent ( i.e., CH2Cl2) dramatically 
accelerated the reaction (entries 8 and 9). 4 -Benzyloxy-TEMPO 
(27c)[36,37] was found to be ideal to promote the formation of 
aldehyde with a good selectivity at C11 ( S/R: 10/1) (entry 10) be -
fore the subsequent HWE reaction.

The reactivity difference between the conjugated ester at C14 
and the isolated ester at C5 may provide enough space for a  
chemoselective reduction. Indeed, when 2.9 equivalents of 
DIBAL-H were introduced, the conjugated methyl ester was pref -
erentially reduced to allylic alcohol , while the isolated ethyl ester 
remained at the aldehyde stage. The resulting 30 was isolated 
with a remarkable 91% yield (Scheme 9). The excellent regioselec-
tivity may be attributed to a favorable six -membered chelation , 
which forms a stable Al -ate complex and thus suppresses the 
further reduction of hemiacetal to alcohol , while the conjugated 
ester is completely reduced to the allylic alcohol. 
Scheme 9  Selective reduction of diester 10 
 
With a sufficient amount of 30 in hand, we then decided to 
introduce the C2 -C5 dienone motif via an HWE elongation. It is 
also interesting to find that the crude product 30 from the reduc-
tion was suitable for the subsequent HWE reaction with phos-
phonate 9a and 9b[38] to form diene -ethyl ester 31a and diene - 
methyl ester 31b with good yield and excellent E,E-stereoselec-
tivity ( ≥13/1) (Scheme 10). The different esters 9a/9b were de -
signed for the future hydrolysis ( vida infra, Scheme 14). The oxi -
dation of allylic alco hol by Dess –Martin periodinane (DMP) [39] 
proceeded well to deliver enal 32 at a high yield without the de -
terioration of the Z-C12-alkene configuration and the stereo -
chemistry at C11. 
Fragment coupling 
With the successful construction of the two complex f rag-
ments 21 and 32, the final installation of the skipped diene linker 
was executed to complete the construction of the whole carbon 
framework. The Lee group first introduced an iterative Julia - 
Kocienski olefination process (repeating a three -step protocol: 
thiolation -oxidation-Julia reaction), which became a standard
